string-array.name: card_facts
string-array.item: Playing cards reached Europe in the 1370s, most likely brought over from the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt.
The four French suits—spades, hearts, diamonds and clubs—appeared in France around 1480 and went on to conquer most of the world.
Italian and Spanish decks still use the older Latin suits: cups, coins, swords and batons.
German decks use hearts, bells, leaves and acorns instead of the French suits.
Swiss-German cards have their own suits: roses, bells, acorns and shields.
A standard deck has 52 cards, and 52 is also the number of weeks in a year.
Add up every card from Ace (1) to King (13) in all four suits and you get 364. Count one Joker as 1 and you get 365.
There are more ways to order a shuffled deck (about 8 × 10⁶⁷) than there are atoms on Earth.
Any thoroughly shuffled deck is almost certainly in an order that no deck has ever been in before.
The mathematicians Bayer and Diaconis showed that about seven riffle shuffles are enough to mix a 52-card deck well.
A perfect \"out\" riffle shuffle, done eight times in a row, puts a 52-card deck back in its original order.
The Joker was added to American decks in the 1860s as the top trump in the game of Euchre.
The King of Hearts is the only King without a moustache on most standard decks.
The King of Hearts is often called the \"suicide king\" because his sword appears to go through his head.
The Jack of Spades, Jack of Hearts and King of Diamonds are shown in profile, so they are nicknamed \"one-eyed\" cards.
In French decks, the Kings were traditionally named David, Alexander, Caesar and Charlemagne.
The Queens of the traditional Paris pattern were named Pallas, Judith, Rachel and Argine.
The Jacks of the Paris pattern were named after heroes: Ogier, La Hire, Hector and Lancelot.
The Jack was once called the Knave. Printers switched to \"J\" so its index wouldn\'t be confused with the King\'s \"K\".
Corner indices, the small rank and suit in each corner, only became common in the late 1800s. Before that, you had to fan cards wide to read them.
Double-ended court cards, readable either way up, became popular in the 1800s so players didn\'t have to turn cards over and reveal their hand.
The ornate Ace of Spades comes from a British tax: from 1765 it was printed by the government to prove the duty had been paid.
The Tarot began in 15th-century Italy as a card game, tarocchi. Its use for fortune-telling came centuries later.
Tarot card games are still played today, especially French Tarot, which is popular in France.
Solitaire is called \"Patience\" in Britain and much of Europe.
The first known collections of patience games were published in the 1870s.
Klondike is named after the Klondike Gold Rush in Canada\'s Yukon, 1896–1899.
Windows 3.0 shipped with Solitaire in 1990, partly to teach people how to use a mouse by dragging and dropping.
FreeCell became famous through Windows, which numbered its deals from 1 to 32,000.
Of Windows\' original 32,000 FreeCell deals, only one, deal #11982, cannot be solved.
Accordion is one of the hardest solitaires to win: a well-played game still fails most of the time.
The mathematician Persi Diaconis called the odds of winning Klondike \"one of the embarrassments of applied probability\": they are still only known by estimate.
Card games were so popular in medieval Europe that many cities passed laws banning them, starting from the 1370s.
The earliest playing cards are thought to come from China, during the Tang dynasty, around the 9th century.
Mamluk cards had suits of cups, coins, swords and polo sticks.
In early European decks, court cards were often three men: a King, a Knight and a Knave. The Queen came later.
Spanish decks traditionally have no 10s, and often no 8s or 9s either.
Cards were among the first things printed with woodblocks in Europe, before Gutenberg\'s press.
Casinos drill holes through, or clip the corners of, retired cards so they can\'t be slipped back into a game.
The world record for the tallest house of cards, built without glue, is more than 7 metres high.
\"Poker face\", \"above board\" and \"ace up your sleeve\" all come from card playing.
\"Following suit\" comes from trick-taking games, where you must play a card of the suit that was led.
The cribbage board of the WWII submarine USS Wahoo is still passed down to the oldest submarine serving in the US Navy.
The standard card size used by casinos is 2.5 × 3.5 inches, called \"poker size\". Narrower \"bridge size\" cards are 2.25 inches wide.
Mahjong grew out of Chinese card games in the 1800s, and its tiles still carry the old card suits of coins, strings and myriads.
In Britain, a deck of cards is usually called a \"pack\".
Kings, Queens and Jacks were once called \"coat cards\", after their fine clothes. The name drifted into \"court cards\".
There are 2,598,960 different five-card poker hands.
The odds of being dealt a royal flush in five cards are 1 in 649,740.
There are about 5.36 × 10²⁸ different ways to deal the four hands of a bridge game.
Card makers traditionally decorate the Ace of Spades with their own name or logo.
The Nine of Diamonds is known as the \"Curse of Scotland\", though nobody is quite sure why.
The Four of Clubs is nicknamed \"the devil\'s bedposts\" and is said by some players to be unlucky.
A tarot deck has 78 cards: 56 in four suits, plus 22 trumps.
In French Tarot, the Fool works a little like a Joker: it can be played instead of following suit.
Japanese hanafuda cards have 12 suits, one for each month of the year, with flowers in place of numbers.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 to make hanafuda playing cards.
During World War II, a US card maker produced decks that came apart when soaked, revealing escape maps for prisoners of war.
Rounded corners became standard in the late 1800s. They wear better than square ones and make a deck easier to shuffle.
Patterned card backs became common in the 1800s. Before that, backs were usually left plain.
Microsoft Solitaire was inducted into the World Video Game Hall of Fame in 2019.
The card designs in Windows Solitaire were drawn by Susan Kare, who also designed the original Macintosh icons.
Napoleon is said to have played patience during his exile on St Helena, and several games are named after him.
Braille playing cards have the rank and suit embossed in a corner so they can be read by touch.
\"Wild card\", \"hold all the cards\" and \"lay your cards on the table\" are all phrases borrowed from card games.
Italy still has many regional card patterns, such as Neapolitan, Piacentine and Sicilian, each with its own look.
The oldest complete deck of ordinary playing cards known is the Flemish Hunting Deck, painted around 1475–1480. Its suits are hunting gear: horns, dog collars, hound tethers and game nooses.
The Stuttgart Playing Cards, painted around 1430, have suits of ducks, falcons, stags and hounds.
The Worshipful Company of Makers of Playing Cards was founded in London by royal charter in 1628, and still exists.
In 1805, an Englishman named Richard Harding was hanged for forging the Ace of Spades to dodge the tax on cards.
Britain\'s tax on playing cards lasted until 1960. The United States had one too, repealed in 1965.
In 1685, the colony of New France ran short of coins and paid its soldiers with playing cards signed by the governor.
During the French Revolution, card makers replaced Kings, Queens and Jacks with Geniuses, Liberties and Equalities.
The Ace was once the lowest card. Its rise above the King is often linked to the French Revolution, though some games ranked it high long before.
The word \"ace\" comes from the Latin \"as\", a small Roman coin, by way of the Old French word for the one on a die.
In French, the suits are pique (pike), cœur (heart), carreau (tile) and trèfle (clover).
The English suit names are borrowed from the older Latin suits: \"spade\" from the Italian for swords, and \"club\" from the batons, though the shapes are French.
French court cards are marked R, D and V, for Roi, Dame and Valet. German ones are K, D and B, for König, Dame and Bube.
In German-suited decks, the Two is called the Daus and usually outranks the King, as an Ace would.
Spanish cards tell you their suit by the breaks in the border line: none for coins, one for cups, two for swords, three for batons.
Indian Ganjifa cards are round and traditionally painted by hand. The Mughal version has 96 cards in eight suits.
Playing cards reached Japan with Portuguese sailors in the 1500s. The Japanese word for cards, \"karuta\", comes from the Portuguese \"carta\".
Tarot trumps were first called \"trionfi\", meaning triumphs. That is where the word \"trump\" comes from.
The Visconti-Sforza decks, painted by hand for the rulers of Milan in the mid-1400s, are among the oldest tarot cards to survive.
Fortune-telling with cards spread in 18th-century France. A Parisian known as Etteilla published the first guide to it in 1770.
The word \"Joker\" is thought to come from \"Jucker\", a German name for the game of Euchre.
In Euchre, the top trumps are Jacks, called \"bowers\" after \"Bauer\", the German word for farmer and a name for the Jack.
The King of Diamonds is the only King who carries an axe instead of a sword.
The Queen of Spades is the only Queen who holds a sceptre.
The first cards with corner indices were nicknamed \"squeezers\", because a hand could be squeezed into a tight fan and still be read.
Bicycle playing cards have been printed since 1885, and were named during the cycling craze of the time.
Bee playing cards, a casino favourite, are marked \"No. 92\" after the year they were first made: 1892.
Most playing cards are two sheets of paper glued together with a dark paste, which stops light from showing through.
The finish on many decks is a pattern of tiny dimples. They hold a little air, which helps the cards glide over each other.
Decks are often printed on sheets of 56 cards: the 52, two Jokers and two extras, which is why so many decks come with spare cards.
\"Transformation\" cards, popular in the 1800s, work the pips into a picture: hearts become faces, spades become hats.
Spell out the thirteen ranks, from \"ace\" to \"king\", and count the letters: there are exactly 52.
Some see a calendar in the deck: four suits for the seasons, 13 cards a suit for the weeks in each, 12 court cards for the months. It is almost certainly a coincidence.
If a deck had been shuffled once a second since the Big Bang, fewer than 10¹⁸ of its 8 × 10⁶⁷ possible orders would have come up.
A \"faro\" shuffle weaves the two halves of a deck together perfectly, one card at a time.
Deal through two shuffled decks side by side, and there is a 63% chance that the same card turns up in both at the same moment.
In bridge, the suits rank in alphabetical order: clubs, diamonds, hearts, spades.
A bridge deal in which every player holds a whole suit is reported every few years. The odds against it are so vast that poor shuffling, or a prank, is the likelier cause.
The name \"bridge\" probably comes from \"biritch\", the name of a whist-like game described in an English pamphlet of 1886.
Poker grew up along the Mississippi in the early 1800s, and was first played with only 20 cards.
\"Dead man\'s hand\", two black Aces and two black Eights, is said to be what Wild Bill Hickok held when he was shot in 1876.
The Texas Legislature officially recognises the town of Robstown as the birthplace of Texas Hold\'em.
\"Passing the buck\" comes from poker, where a marker called the buck, often a knife with a buckhorn handle, showed whose turn it was to deal.
The earliest known mention of the game twenty-one is in a story by Cervantes, the author of Don Quixote, written around 1601.
In blackjack, a two-card 21 turns up about once in every 21 hands.
Crazy Eights is said to be named after \"Section 8\", the US military\'s discharge for soldiers judged mentally unfit.
Scopa, the Italian card game, means \"broom\": the best move is to sweep every card off the table.
In Dickens\'s Great Expectations, Pip and Estella play Beggar-my-neighbour. Whether a game of it could go on forever was an open question until 2024, when a never-ending deal was found.
Paul Cézanne\'s painting The Card Players was reported sold for more than $250 million in 2011, then the highest price ever paid for a painting.
\"Dogs Playing Poker\" is really a series: Cassius Coolidge painted 16 pictures of dogs for a firm that advertised cigars, starting in 1903.
During the Vietnam War, American soldiers asked card makers for crates of nothing but Aces of Spades, believing, wrongly, that the enemy feared the card.
Several US states give prisoners decks printed with unsolved cases, and tips from the players have solved crimes.
The record for throwing a playing card is 65.96 metres, set by the magician Rick Smith Jr. in 2002.
The record for memorising the order of a shuffled deck is under 13 seconds.
Bryan Berg, who holds the records for houses of cards, trained as an architect. He uses no glue, tape or folds.
The oldest known description of a patience game is in a German book of games from 1783.
In Britain, \"solitaire\" usually means the board game with pegs. The card games are \"patience\".
The stock, the pile of cards left over after the deal, is also called the \"talon\", French for \"heel\".
Canfield is named after Richard Canfield, a casino owner said to have sold players a deck for $50 and paid $5 for every card they got to the foundations.
Spider Solitaire takes its name from a spider\'s eight legs: there are eight foundations to fill.
Forty Thieves is named after the 40 cards dealt to the tableau at the start. It is also known as Napoleon at St Helena.
Calculation is a solitaire of almost pure skill: a careful player can win most games, where a careless one wins almost none.
Windows Solitaire once had a \"boss key\" that hid the game behind a fake spreadsheet. Microsoft had it taken out before release.
Windows FreeCell hid two deals numbered −1 and −2, which were built to be impossible.
Hearts was added to Windows in 1992 to show off its new networking: it could be played against people on other computers.
In 2020, on Solitaire\'s 30th birthday, Microsoft said the game still had 35 million players a month.
